p:cNvPr.descr: Photograph and diagrams of inward curvature of the cell membrane by calveolin. (a) Top. A black-and-white microscopic image of a cell membrane. The membrane is toward the bottom and is dark gray. The calveola of the membrane can be seen as a small inverted bulb shaped invaginations along the membrane. They are dark gray. (b) Below, an illustration of an calveola of the membrane. The membrane has blue edges and a yellow center. It is labeled at the top left. The cytosol below it is yellow. The membrane calveola inward, forming a pocket labeled “calveola.” The outside and inside of the membrane are labeled on the right. The inside of the membrane of the calveola is lined by small red and purple proteins, which are the calveolins. A bottom portion of the calveola diagram is boxed with a large white arrow pointing down. Below, a close-up illustration of the interaction of calveolin with the cell membrane. It is inside a large box. The membrane has blue and green heads on the outside surface and blue and purple heads on the inside surface. The calveolin dimer is a pair of thin pale purple chains that bonds to the inner surface of the membrane and pull it inward. The bond to the membrane and curve upward to interrupt the yellow hydrophobic tails. Red zigzagged lines extend up into the membrane from the left and right sides of the calveolin, cementing the attachment. Text to the bottom left of the calveolin reads, “Caveolin dimer (six fatty acyl, eight cholesterol moieties).” (c) Below is an illustration showing the flattening and expanding of the membrane. On the left is a calveola, its bulb shaded green and the flatter membrane to the left and right shaded gray. The calveola is labeled in the middle. The cytosol below it is pale yellow. Text reading “mechanical stress” with a left and right arrow is above this image. To the right is an arrow showing an illustration of the calveola stretched into an expanded surface; the green section of the calveola is now flat and in line with the gray sections. It is labeled “expanded surface.” Below this is a simple illustration of a cell, labeled in the center, with multiple calveolae all around its circumference. The calveolae are green and the rest of the membrane is gray. A right arrow points to a cell with no calveolae and its surface expanded. The cell is considerably larger, having increased in volume but decreased surface area. It is labeled “enlarged cell” in the center.
